specPoints.text: be able to deduce the order (0, 1 or 2) with respect to a substance in a rate equation, using data from: i a concentration-time graph ii a rate-concentration graph iii an initial-rate method

primer.text: The initial-rate method finds the rate at the very start by drawing a tangent at t = 0, or more conveniently by timing a single visual change in a clock reaction. This note calculates an initial rate from a tangent, converts measured times into proportional rates through 1/t, and states the constant-rate assumption the clock method depends on.

lessons.title: Tangents at the start
lessons.opening: The initial-rate method reads the rate at the very start, when concentrations are known and side effects have not yet accumulated. Draw the concentration-time curve, lay a tangent at t = 0, and its gradient is the initial rate. Clock reactions shortcut the whole curve with one timed visual change.
keyPoints: The initial rate is determined at the very start of the reaction, at t = 0.
The tangent method draws a concentration-time graph, adds a tangent at t = 0, and calculates the gradient of that tangent.
For calcium carbonate with hydrochloric acid, gas volumes are measured for several acid concentrations and each curve gains a starting tangent.
Clock reactions time a single visual change - a colour change or precipitate - and take the initial rate as proportional to 1/t.
Clock reactions assume no significant rate change between mixing and the measured moment.

low.restatement: Initial rate = gradient of the tangent at t = 0; the clock shortcut times one visual change and uses 1/t.
low.analogy: Sprinting out of the blocks: the opening stride speed is the initial rate, measured before fatigue (falling concentrations) sets in.
low.examPointer: Always state the tangent's rise and run before quoting the gradient - examiners want the working.

medium.restatement: Early data are the cleanest: concentrations are at their starting values, so the tangent at zero time reflects the rate equation in its purest form; clock reactions trade the whole curve for one honest stopwatch reading.
medium.analogy: Judging a car's acceleration from the first second off the line, before traffic and hills interfere.
medium.examPointer: The 1/t rule is a proportionality, not an equality - say 'proportional to' when you use it.

check.stem: The initial rate of a reaction is measured

options.text: At the very start of the reaction, at t = 0
options.explanation: Initial means before any significant concentration change.
Midpoint times give average, not initial, rates.
No rate information survives completion.

options.text: At the steepest point of the curve only
options.explanation: The steepest point may occur later; initial means t = 0.

check.stem: The tangent method for finding an initial rate involves

options.text: Drawing a tangent to the concentration-time curve at t = 0 and computing its gradient
options.explanation: The starting gradient is the initial rate.
Endpoints carry no rate information.
That describes the clock method.
No such quotient exists.

check.stem: In the calcium carbonate and hydrochloric acid demonstration, tangents are added because

options.text: Each acid concentration gives its own curve, and each starting gradient is that run's initial rate
options.explanation: One tangent per curve reads one initial rate.

options.text: The curves are all straight lines
options.explanation: Curved or straight, tangents give the starting rate.

options.text: The gas volume is too small to read
options.explanation: Volume readability is not the reason.
Drawing tangents changes nothing physically.

check.stem: A clock reaction measures the time t for a visual change, and the initial rate is taken as

options.explanation: Faster changes mean shorter times, so inverse proportionality.
That would make slower reactions have larger rates.
No square relationship applies.
The timing is the whole measurement.

check.stem: The key assumption behind clock reactions is that

options.text: The rate stays roughly constant between mixing and the moment the clock change is seen
options.explanation: The 1/t conversion presumes a steady early rate.

options.text: The rate rises steeply throughout the run
options.explanation: That would break the method.

options.text: The visual change happens by itself
options.explanation: The change marks a fixed extent of reaction.
Temperature is held constant.

check.stem: State how a tangent yields an initial rate.
check.modelAnswer: Draw the tangent at t = 0 on the concentration-time graph and calculate its gradient; that gradient is the initial rate.

check.stem: State what a clock reaction times and how the initial rate is taken from it.
check.modelAnswer: It times the moment of a single visual change, and the initial rate is taken as proportional to 1/t.

check.stem: Explain why the tangent at t = 0 gives the cleanest reading of the rate equation.
check.modelAnswer: At the start, concentrations equal the values the experimenter chose, so the measured gradient corresponds to known concentrations without any drift; later points mix changing concentrations into the reading.

check.stem: A clock reaction records 25 s for the colour change at one concentration and 50 s at half that concentration. What does the comparison suggest about the order?
check.modelAnswer: Halving the concentration doubles the time, so 1/t halves, meaning the rate halved with the concentration - behaviour consistent with first order.

lessons.title: Clock data in practice
sourceHeadings: Specimen Results for the Iodine Clock Reaction Table
lessons.opening: A specimen iodine-clock table lists concentrations and the times at which the colour appeared. Converting each time to 1/t gives proportional rates, and the pattern across the table - doubling concentration doubling the rate - hands over the order directly.
keyPoints: The specimen iodine clock table pairs concentrations with the measured times for the visual change.
Each initial rate scales with 1/t; at 0.01515 mol dm-3 the rate works out as 1/40 = 0.025 s^-1.
As concentration doubles the rate doubles, which links the clock data to a first-order reaction.
Short measured times give more accurate initial rates; long times drift from the true starting rate.

low.restatement: Convert each time to 1/t, compare across the table, and read the order from how rate tracks concentration.
low.analogy: A queue where service speed is judged by waiting time: half the waiting means double the throughput.
low.examPointer: Show one worked conversion (1/40 = 0.025) and one doubling comparison - that is the full method.

medium.restatement: Because clock timing measures the same visual milestone every run, 1/t is a rate ruler; ratios of 1/t values are ratios of initial rates.
medium.analogy: Timing identical races over the same distance: finishing times compare speeds directly.
medium.examPointer: Note the accuracy caveat: short times are honest, long times understate the true initial rate.

check.stem: The initial rate proportional to 1/t for a measured time of 40 s is

options.explanation: That is t, not 1/t.
A decimal slip of the true quotient.
That is 1/0.04, mixing units.

check.stem: The specimen clock table shows the rate doubling when concentration doubles, which identifies the reaction as

options.text: First order with respect to that reactant
options.explanation: Doubling on doubling is the proportionality signature.
Zero order would show no rate change.
Second order would quadruple the rate.
Third order would give an eightfold rise.

check.stem: Clock-reaction initial rates become less accurate when the measured time is long because

options.text: The constant-rate assumption weakens as reactants deplete during the long wait
options.explanation: Drifting concentrations break the 1/t shortcut.
Timing devices are not the issue.
The endpoint is fixed, not strengthened.
The quotient is always defined for positive t.

check.stem: In the clock table, 1/t values across different concentrations can be compared directly because

options.text: Each 1/t carries the same proportionality to its run's initial rate
options.explanation: The same milestone and assumption apply to every run.

options.text: The units of 1/t change with concentration
options.explanation: Units stay s^-1 throughout.

options.text: Each run used a different indicator
options.explanation: One indicator system is used throughout.
Runs are held at fixed temperature.

check.stem: A clock run records a much longer time than the others in its set. The best inference is

options.text: Its initial rate is the smallest and the least accurate of the set
options.explanation: Long times mean slow early rates and weakening assumptions.

options.text: Its initial rate is the largest
options.explanation: Large rates give short times.
The endpoint was still reached.
Higher concentration shortens the time.

check.stem: State the 1/t conversion for a measured time of 40 s.
check.modelAnswer: 1/40 = 0.025 s^-1, the quantity proportional to the initial rate.

check.stem: State the accuracy trend of clock-reaction rates as measured times lengthen.
check.modelAnswer: Accuracy falls: short times give initial rates close to the true value, long times drift from it.

check.stem: Explain why 1/t can serve as a stand-in for the initial rate in clock experiments.
check.modelAnswer: Every run triggers the same small extent of reaction before the clock change appears, so the distance travelled is fixed and speed equals that fixed extent divided by time, making rate proportional to 1/t.

check.stem: Two clock runs give times of 20 s and 40 s. State the ratio of their initial rates.
check.modelAnswer: The rates are proportional to 1/20 and 1/40, so the faster run's initial rate is twice the slower run's.

glossary.definition: The rate right at the reaction's start, read off the tangent drawn at t = 0.
A method timing one visual change, with initial rate proportional to 1/t.
A straight line touching a curve at one point whose gradient gives the instantaneous rate.

workedExample.prompt: From the concentration-time graph for calcium carbonate with 2.0 mol dm^-3 hydrochloric acid, the tangent drawn at t = 0 rises 42 units while running 38 units along the time axis. Calculate the initial rate.
steps: Apply the gradient formula: rise divided by run.
Round to three figures and attach the axis units.
workedExample.finalAnswer: The initial rate is 1.10 mol dm^-3 s^-1.
